response = "The question was settled by two complementary experimental strategies: a biological transformation assay in bacteria combined with enzymes of defined substrate specificity, and radioisotopic tracing of the molecules that enter a host cell during infection. In both programmes the logic was subtractive, in that the candidate molecule whose destruction destroys biological activity, and whose atoms enter the cell, is the one that carries the information. Before 1944, proteins were widely regarded as the most likely carriers of heredity. That expectation resulted directly from Phoebus Levene's tetranucleotide hypothesis, which depicted DNA as a monotonous repeating structure. That non-virulent pneumococci could be converted into virulent forms, which Frederick Griffith reported in 1928, is confirmed by his transformation experiments, which used strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae injected into mice. Sixteen years after that report of 1928, Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty published their identification of the pneumococcal transforming principle in 1944; by contrast with the protein-centred consensus that had dominated the field, their identification located the hereditary activity in a different class of molecule altogether. The decisive step in the pneumococcal system was enzymatic rather than purely chemical, since purification alone leaves trace contaminants in dispute. The destruction of activity by an enzyme that cleaves deoxyribonucleic acid and nothing else cannot be squared with an identification of the transforming principle as ribonucleic acid, and rules that identification out. A second and independent line of attack used bacteriophage, where the protein coat and the nucleic acid core can be tagged with different isotopes and then physically separated by blending and centrifugation. The Hershey-Chase experiment labelled bacteriophage DNA with phosphorus-32. The Hershey-Chase experiment labelled phage nucleic acid with carbon-14. A phosphorus-32 tag on the phage DNA excludes a carbon-14 tag on that same phage nucleic acid, because the two labelling schemes cannot both have been the one applied to the molecule under test. Most of the phosphorus-32 radioactivity was recovered inside the infected bacterial cells rather than in the stripped coats left outside them. That partition of the isotope between host cytoplasm and discarded protein shell shows that DNA is the molecule that carries hereditary information in cells; in other words, the genetic material of cells is deoxyribonucleic acid. The force of the result lies in its quantitative character: the material that directs the production of progeny particles is the material that physically enters the cell, and that material is traced by the phosphorus label."
